channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Why this longevity startup raised in Japan, not Silicon Valley | TWiST Tokyo | E2315
gist: Recorded live in Tokyo at Founder University, Jason Calacanis interviews Bilal, founder of longevity-data startup EkiLabs (epigenetics for drug discovery and cell-therapy QC), covering why Japan's regenerative-medicine law and bank-loan-stacked financing make it an attractive base, plus Calacanis's own frameworks on exits, VC power-law math, and founder work ethic.

insights.claim: EkiLabs generates high-resolution, low-cost epigenetic (DNA methylation) data and monetizes it two ways: paid discovery research on aging for pharma/biotech clients, and manufacturing quality control for cell-therapy companies (testing whether stem-cell batches are potent, consistent, and identical batch-to-batch).
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: A picks-and-shovels play in longevity biotech (data infrastructure, not a specific drug candidate) with two distinct near-term revenue lines rather than a single binary drug-development bet.

insights.claim: EkiLabs' founder argues the real moat in AI-for-biology is proprietary data generation, not modeling, because public genomic/epigenetic datasets weren't built for a specific phenotype or clinical indication and models cannot substitute for data that doesn't exist.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating AI-biotech startups should weight proprietary wet-lab data-generation capability over algorithmic sophistication; pure-model biotech startups without their own data pipeline may be structurally disadvantaged.
insights.quote: you cannot really model your way out from a data set that isn't there.

insights.claim: EkiLabs' founder predicts the next frontier in AI biology modeling will be 'virtual cell organisms' -- an AlphaFold-scale breakthrough enabled once enough high-resolution epigenetic/cellular data exists -- which he expects to unlock groundbreaking new drugs.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: Watch for startups building virtual-cell-model platforms as a next wave of AI-biotech investment once enabling datasets mature.

insights.claim: EkiLabs deliberately shut down a revenue-generating, growing service line -- measuring biological age for longevity clinics -- even though it was cash-positive, judging it a distraction from building the higher-value core data-generation platform.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: Illustrates founders trading near-term cash flow for a bigger long-term IP-generating platform bet -- a pattern worth watching for in growth-stage biotech capital-allocation decisions.
insights.quote: we made a difficult choice of cutting a service that was actually generating cash regularly and predictively

insights.claim: According to EkiLabs' founder, an AI-designed drug has already reached Phase 3 in the regulatory process, indicating AI-driven drug design is moving from hype into late-stage clinical review.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: A concrete de-risking milestone for the AI-drug-discovery investment thesis, though unnamed and secondhand so should be corroborated before acting on it.

themes.theme: Longevity science and Japan's regulatory arbitrage

insights.claim: The first clinical trials aiming at potentially reversing aging come from Life Biosciences (Dr. David Sinclair) and NewLimit (funded by Coinbase's Brian Armstrong), with NewLimit's first clinical trial hoped for within the next year.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: Concrete names to track for anti-aging clinical-trial catalysts; shows non-traditional (crypto-founder) capital flowing into longevity biotech.

insights.claim: Japan is unusually favorable for regenerative-medicine startups because its 2013 Regenerative Medicine Law -- enacted after Dr. Shinya Yamanaka's 2012 Nobel Prize for induced pluripotent stem cells -- fast-tracks cell and gene therapies, giving Japan access to treatments unavailable under the more conservative US FDA regime.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: A regulatory-arbitrage opportunity: biotech investors/founders can access faster clinical-validation pathways for cell/gene therapies in Japan than in the US.

insights.claim: EkiLabs located its R&D lab specifically in Okinawa to access the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) -- a Prime Minister's Office-run, English-language institute that is 50% Japanese/50% foreign PhD-level talent -- rather than for the region's 'blue zone' longevity branding.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
entities: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology
insights.so_what: Illustrates a talent-arbitrage strategy: elite research institutes outside traditional biotech hubs can supply lower-cost, world-class science talent.

insights.claim: EkiLabs' founder supports expanding 'right to try' laws (which let terminally ill patients access unapproved cell/gene therapies) and personally believes even healthy people should be allowed to try unapproved longevity therapies at their own risk, while acknowledging the ethical difficulty this poses for doctors.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: Watch state-level 'right to try' legislation as a potential faster, alternative commercialization channel for longevity/cell-therapy companies that bypasses full FDA approval.

insights.claim: Blue-zone longevity claims have been partly discredited: a widely discussed paper found many purported 'blue zones' coincide with the poorest, worst-documented regions, where some people recorded as reaching 100 years old had actually already died, with families continuing to collect their pension.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: Caution against overpaying for 'blue zone' narrative-driven longevity/wellness products; investors should distinguish biomarker-validated aging science from unverified demographic folklore.
insights.quote: some people for example that we estimated to be 100 years were just dead

insights.claim: Emerging research cited in the conversation links bilingual or multilingual fluency to dramatically lower rates of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, suggesting cognitive 'exercise' via language plasticity may be an underexplored longevity lever alongside socialization and diet.
insights.speaker: host and guest
insights.so_what: A potential future consumer or therapeutic angle (cognitive-training products) within the broader longevity market beyond biomarkers and drugs.

insights.claim: EkiLabs' founder frames 'biological age' as fundamentally a cohort-benchmarking exercise -- comparing an individual's biomarker pattern (e.g., DNA methylation) to people of known chronological age -- rather than one absolute truth, which is why different tests (wearables vs. blood panels) can disagree.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: Consumers and investors should treat consumer biological-age scores as directionally noisy proxies rather than clinical-grade metrics, unlike cohort-validated biomarkers used in drug development.

insights.claim: Optimizing consumer wearable or biomarker scores (e.g., gaming a fixed sleep schedule for a better Whoop score) can become disconnected from actual health outcomes, and some companies have begun tracking employees' biological age as an early-warning signal for burnout.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: An emerging enterprise use case: biological-age monitoring as a corporate HR/wellness tool to flag burnout risk before attrition occurs.

insights.claim: Japanese biotech/deep-tech startups can stack non-dilutive capital -- seed equity from Japanese VCs/angels plus low-interest, government-guaranteed regional bank loans to startups -- letting EkiLabs deploy more capital than what it raised in equity while keeping a clean cap table.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: US investors comparing headline equity-raise sizes for Japanese startups may be underestimating true capital deployed via government-backed bank debt.

insights.claim: Angel check sizes in Japan range from a few thousand dollars up to roughly $100k-$200k, materially smaller than typical US angel checks, but this is offset by a much lower cost of running a startup in Japan than in San Francisco.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: Sets up a capital-efficiency arbitrage: US biotech VCs are reportedly surprised by how much small-check Japanese startups accomplish, implying attractive risk-adjusted entry valuations abroad.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis argues US startup valuations have again become 'disconnected from reality' (comparing today to 2019-2020 and the SaaS-era bubble), creating an arbitrage opportunity to find capital-efficient teams internationally at lower valuations before structuring a later flip to a US entity for exit.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A cross-border early-stage investing thesis: seek undervalued non-US teams and plan for eventual US redomiciliation ('the flip') ahead of exit.

insights.claim: EkiLabs is currently incorporated in Japan but is in talks with US VCs about 'flipping' to a Delaware entity to access larger, less cost-sensitive American capital ahead of a prospective exit or IPO.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: A repeatable template for foreign biotech founders: incorporate cheaply and locally early, then flip to Delaware to unlock US growth capital later.

insights.claim: The 'Japanese Series B' historically functioned as a de facto IPO, with companies going public on the Tokyo Stock Exchange with as little as $5-10M in revenue, but the exchange tightened this after too many resulting 'zombie companies,' and Japan is now restructuring to encourage M&A as an alternative exit path.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: Implies a growth-capital gap in Japan around the Series B/C stage -- an opening for growth-equity investors to fill the void left by a stricter IPO bar.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis notes US M&A activity slowed materially during the Biden administration under FTC chair Lina Khan's aggressive antitrust enforcement, but has picked back up under the Trump administration's more permissive, personally-involved stance on approving deals.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Signals a more permissive US M&A environment for startup exits, a tailwind for VC-backed company liquidity, albeit with fairness/impartiality concerns Calacanis flags himself.

themes.theme: Founder decisions on exits and VC math

insights.claim: Calacanis frames three legitimate reasons to sell a startup: the founder has lost personal drive to run it daily; the company receives a life-changing, 'unreasonable' offer far above its last valuation; or an acquirer can dramatically accelerate the mission with resources the founder alone couldn't access -- while founders should never signal to their own investors that they want a quick exit, since VC portfolio math depends on power-law outliers.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A concrete heuristic founders and investors can apply directly when negotiating exit timing and board messaging.
insights.quote: Great companies are bought, not sold.

insights.claim: Calacanis explains VC power-law math concretely: a $200M fund investing in 30 companies expects roughly 25 to go to zero, three to return 2-3x, and one or two to be outliers; a fund owning 10% ($2M) of a $20M-valuation company that grows to a $10B outcome, diluted to a 5% final stake, nets $500M, making it a 2.5x fund off that single deal.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A useful mental model for founders facing board pressure toward growth-at-all-costs versus an earlier, modest exit.

insights.claim: Calacanis relays that a company with multiple competing acquisition offers (e.g., a formal process narrowing 12 initial targets down to final bids) commands a premium price, whereas a company that actively shops itself for sale signals weakness and depresses the price it gets.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Unsolicited inbound acquisition interest is a leading indicator of a company's strategic value, worth watching before any formal sale process becomes public.
insights.quote: If you're in the selling process and trying to convince people, it's going to go for a low price. If you have multiple offers, it's going to go for a high price

insights.claim: EkiLabs' founder frames its own sell-vs-hold decision as whether staying independent lets the company keep compounding its IP/data-asset value ('the engine to generate IP') faster than a lump-sum acquisition offer would be worth.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: A model for founders to weigh a 'keep building vs. sell now' comparison rather than reacting emotionally to acquisition interest.

insights.claim: Calacanis describes Amazon's 'bar raiser' hiring philosophy -- deliberately hiring people whose domain knowledge exceeds anyone currently on the team, even though existing staff may fear being outshone -- as core to strong early-stage team-building, citing EkiLabs' engineering hires as an example.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A concrete hiring rubric investors can check portfolio companies against when assessing team quality and talent density.

insights.claim: EkiLabs is deliberately 'AI 1.0' internally -- no AI agents or cron jobs running the company, given heavy manual lab work -- but hires junior ML-background staff specifically because they can use AI tools to multiply senior engineers' output to world-class level.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: A contrarian data point against assuming AI-native biotech companies are automatically AI-run operationally -- many remain lab/manual-labor bound despite an AI-heavy end product.

insights.claim: Japanese employees have historically undervalued equity compensation (viewing stock options as a lottery ticket rather than a wealth-building tool, unlike Silicon Valley's cutthroat equity-driven job-hopping culture), though this is shifting as Japan recently eased stock-option taxation and regulation.
insights.speaker: Bilal, EkiLabs founder
insights.so_what: Signals a maturing equity culture in Japan could raise talent-retention/competition costs for Japanese startups over time as employees become more equity-savvy.

insights.claim: Calacanis argues efficiency, not raw hours, is the primary lever for founder productivity -- citing his own ruthless time management (batching decisions, rejecting sales calls, requiring recorded video pitches) -- while criticizing extreme low-sleep hustle culture (citing a report that Japan's prime minister sleeps 0-3 hours a night) as unsustainable and error-inducing.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A practical operating heuristic for founders on time allocation, and a signal that Calacanis treats extreme sleep deprivation as a red flag in founders he backs.
insights.quote: efficiency can beat hours but efficiency and hours can beat everything

insights.claim: Calacanis argues compounding weekly improvement (kaizen) is undervalued relative to compounding financial interest, and that in the current competitive environment 'a week you don't grow exponentially is a week you might waste forever,' raising the bar for acceptable startup pace versus prior eras.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Signals that VC growth-cadence expectations for portfolio companies have tightened -- slower iteration is penalized more heavily than in past cycles.

top_entities: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology
